title: Post-Soviet Birthplaces in Sarasota County
text:
Estimated population change
The chart compares each country’s earliest and latest available estimate. Bars show estimated change; whiskers show an approximate margin of error for the difference. Changes within or near the whiskers are especially uncertain. Even changes outside them are not definitive significance tests because ACS five-year periods overlap.

title: About this project
text: The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991 into 15 independent republics with distinct languages, cultures, and histories. This project focuses on those birthplaces to explore one small, local part of that larger story: what public Census data can tell us about Sarasota County residents born in those places. “Post-Soviet” is a historical and geographic description, not a single identity or migration experience.

title: About this project
text:
What the Census measures
The chart uses the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey (ACS) five-year estimates for Sarasota County, Florida, from the B05006 place-of-birth table. The table estimates the foreign-born population by place of birth. It does not measure ancestry, ethnicity, language, immigration status, or how a person identifies.
Each plotted value is an estimate for an ACS five-year period ending in the year shown. For example, 2024 is the 2020–2024 ACS five-year estimate, not a count taken only in 2024. Adjacent five-year periods overlap substantially and are not independent snapshots.

title: About this project
text:
Country availability and regional groupings
The dashboard lists all 15 former Soviet republics. The ACS does not publish separate estimates for all of them in every period. In the data used here, Azerbaijan and Georgia have separate estimates starting in 2022; Estonia, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan are not separately reported. Missing estimates are left blank, never treated as zero.
The regional comparison uses these project-defined groupings:

These are groupings for this dashboard, not Census regions. Each period’s regional total includes only member countries with a separate estimate in that period. Hover over a regional line to see how many countries were reported. The combined regional margin of error is approximated by the square root of the sum of squared country margins of error, which assumes independent country estimates; it is not an official Census regional estimate.

title: About this project
text:
Comparing changes and uncertainty
For each country with at least two reported periods, the change chart subtracts its earliest available estimate from its latest available estimate. The plotted change margin of error is approximated as:
sqrt(earliest-period MOE^2 + latest-period MOE^2)
This approximation treats the endpoint estimates as independent. They are not fully independent when the ACS five-year periods overlap, and the chart does not have the covariance information needed for a formal significance test. Error bars are a reminder of uncertainty, not a guarantee that a change is real or statistically significant. Small estimates can also have large margins of error.
The total summary card is a sum of the separately reported country estimates for the latest period. It covers only the countries with separate estimates in that period; it is not a complete count for all 15 republics. Its margin of error is also an approximate combination, not an official published total.

title: About this project
section: What these data cannot tell us
text:
What these data cannot tell us
Birthplace estimates do not show U.S.-born descendants, individual migration histories, reasons for moving, refugee or other immigration pathways, community ties, or identity. A place-of-birth category may include people with very different experiences. An estimate of zero is not proof that no residents were born in that place; interpret it alongside its margin of error. These county-level estimates describe a population, not any one person.
